papers.title: Insulin resistance blood markers predict clinical milestones in early-stage Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by clinical heterogeneity and substantial variability in disease course. Insulin resistance (IR) has been proposed as a contributor to PD progression, although its prognostic role remains unclear. We investigated whether blood surrogate markers of IR, the triglyceride/high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio (TG/HDL-C) and triglyceride-glucose index (TyG), could predict the development of clinical milestones (CM) in early-stage PD patients (ePD). MATERIALS AND METHODS: this longitudinal study included 98 ePD patients and 81 matched controls. At baseline, participants underwent clinical examination and blood sampling, allowing calculation of TG/HDL-C and TyG. Patients were followed for at least one year and stratified according to CM occurrence, defined as the first visit at which cognitive impairment, recurrent falls or visual hallucinations were documented. An Elastic Net-penalized Cox model with bootstrap resampling was used to identify robust prognostic variables while minimizing overfitting. Selected variables were then entered into a multivariable Cox proportional hazards model. Time-dependent ROC analysis assessed the prognostic performance of TG/HDL-C. RESULTS: baseline TG/HDL-C levels were significantly higher among patients experiencing CM. Notably, this marker emerged as the only independent predictor of CM development in the multivariable analysis (HR = 2.03, p < 0.001). Higher values were also associated with reduced CM-free survival and showed moderate prognostic discrimination at 60 months (AUC = 0.737), with a cutoff of 1.63 identifying patients at increased risk of CM. CONCLUSION: TG/HDL-C, a surrogate marker of IR, may provide prognostic information and help identify ePD patients at risk of worse disease progression.

papers.title: SV2A PET imaging in Parkinson's disease and atypical parkinsonism: A systematic review of neuroimaging methodologies and regional findings.
papers.abstract: BackgroundReduced presynaptic density, commonly referred to as synaptic loss, is an early and clinically relevant feature of parkinsonian disorders. The development of positron emission tomography (PET) radiotracers targeting synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A) has enabled in vivo quantification of synaptic density.ObjectivesThis systematic review examines neuroimaging methodologies and regional SV2A PET findings in Parkinson's disease (PD), progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), corticobasal degeneration (CBD), and multiple system atrophy (MSA).MethodsA systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science was conducted following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines, including studies employing validated SV2A PET radiotracers to quantify synaptic density in parkinsonian populations. Risk of bias was assessed using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies (QUADAS)-2 tool. Substantial methodological heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis; findings were synthesized narratively.ResultsFourteen studies were included. In PD, the substantia nigra was the most affected region, with striatal involvement more prominent in advanced disease (>6 years duration). In PSP and CBD, synaptic loss was widespread, exceeded grey matter atrophy, and correlated with clinical severity and cognitive decline; longitudinal PSP data showed reductions of approximately 3-4% per year in frontal and caudate regions. In MSA, infratentorial involvement (cerebellum, pons, medulla) predominated, enabling diagnostic differentiation with high accuracy (AUC up to 0.99).ConclusionsSV2A PET reveals disease-specific patterns of reduced presynaptic availability, consistent with synaptic loss, across parkinsonian disorders, supporting its potential as a diagnostic and monitoring biomarker. Methodological harmonization and longitudinal multicenter studies are needed to establish clinical utility.

papers.title: Hsp10 Targets the C-Terminus of α-Synuclein to Inhibit Secondary Nucleation and Remodel Labile Fibrils.
papers.journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
papers.abstract: Aggregation of α-synuclein is a central pathological feature of Parkinson's disease and related synucleinopathies. The co-chaperonin Hsp10, a component of the Hsp60/Hsp10 chaperonin system, has recently been proposed to possess independent chaperone activity and has been found to co-localize with α-synuclein aggregates in diseased brains, suggesting a role in regulating α-synuclein assembly. Here, we combine solution NMR spectroscopy, cryo-electron microscopy, and kinetic analyses to define a multistage mechanism by which Hsp10 modulates α-synuclein aggregation. Hsp10 transiently interacts with monomeric α-synuclein, with residues on the inner surface and top-loop regions of Hsp10 primarily engaging the acidic C-terminal region of α-synuclein. Hsp10 exerts a concentration-dependent, biphasic effect on aggregation, accelerating fibrillization at substoichiometric concentrations while inhibiting de novo aggregation at higher concentrations through suppression of secondary nucleation. Furthermore, Hsp10 decorates fibril surfaces through interactions with the exposed α-synuclein C-terminus, thereby limiting secondary nucleation. Hsp10 also promotes the disaggregation of thermodynamically labile fibrillar fragments. Together, these findings establish a mechanistic framework for Hsp10-mediated regulation of α-synuclein assembly and expand the functional landscape of Hsp10 beyond its canonical role in mitochondrial protein folding.

papers.title: High-Throughput Plasma Proteomic Profiling Identifies Novel Biomarker Candidates in Parkinson's Disease with Cognitive Decline.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a common neurodegenerative disease diagnosed based on its cardinal motor features. Many PD patients experience non-motor symptoms, including cognitive decline, which can be particularly debilitating. Fluid biomarkers in PD are lacking, but modern proteomic techniques have allowed for high-throughput studies which have generated promising results. Mass spectrometry provides an unbiased approach to biomarker discovery, and the plasma proteome reflects ongoing disease processes throughout the body, including the central nervous system. Plasma samples from 198 individuals (130 PD and 68 controls) from the Swedish Biopark cohort were TMT-tagged, pre-fractionated, and analysed using untargeted mass spectrometry. Robust peptides from candidate biomarkers were technically verified using parallel reaction monitoring (PRM). The analyses focused on PD diagnosis and cognitive decline. Results were compared with plasma Neurofilament light chain levels analysed on the SIMOA platform. Several promising candidate biomarkers were discovered for PD diagnosis, cognitive decline, and motor impairment in the discovery phase. Peptides from six of the 12 proteins quantified with PRM correlated with quantifications from the discovery phase. Following PRM verification, it was found that peptides from C9 and APOC3 had altered levels in PD compared with controls. Additionally, SAA1 was found to be associated with both cognitive and motor impairment. Neurofilament light chain levels were elevated in PD with cognitive impairment but showed a weaker correlation with cognitive function than SAA1. In conclusion, untargeted mass spectrometry is a viable method for generating novel candidate biomarkers in PD plasma, several of which were technically verified with PRM including SAA1, C9, and APOC3.

papers.title: Rapid Eye Movement Sleep Behavior Disorder as a Prodromal Manifestation of Alpha-Synucleinopathies.
papers.abstract: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (RBD) is a parasomnia in which patients physically act out their dreams due to loss of the normal muscle paralysis that occurs during REM sleep. It is now recognized that isolated RBD (iRBD) is strongly associated with future development of α-synuclein-related neurodegenerative diseases, including Parkinson disease (PD), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), and multiple system atrophy (MSA). It is seen that most patients with polysomnography-confirmed iRBD eventually develop a clinically defined synucleinopathy, often after a long symptom-free interval. This long prodromal phase makes iRBD a unique clinical model for studying the earliest stages of neurodegeneration, before the onset of clear motor or cognitive disability. α-synuclein pathology frequently begins in the lower brainstem and autonomic nervous system, affecting REM sleep regulatory circuits early in the disease process. As pathology spreads, dopaminergic, cholinergic, and cortical systems become involved, leading to the gradual emergence of motor, autonomic, and cognitive symptoms. As a result, many individuals with iRBD exhibit subtle non-motor features such as hyposmia, constipation, orthostatic hypotension, anxiety, and mild cognitive changes years before a formal neurological diagnosis is made. Recent advances have improved the ability to identify patients at the highest risk of near-term phenoconversion. Quantitative measures of REM sleep without atonia, dopamine transporter imaging, autonomic testing, and emerging molecular biomarkers, including α-synuclein seed amplification assays, have shown promise in risk stratification. In addition, cognitive changes may occur earlier than previously recognized, particularly in patients with iRBD who also demonstrate hyposmia or dopaminergic dysfunction. Management of RBD remains largely symptomatic and focuses on injury prevention and sleep stabilization. While clonazepam and melatonin remain fi

papers.title: Target engagement without clinical benefit: a systematic review, mechanism-concordant meta-analysis, and research agenda for Parkinson's disease immunotherapy.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Immune-based and inflammation-targeted therapies have strong biological rationale in Parkinson's disease (PD). We re-examined this translational gap using a tiered evidence framework and mechanism-concordant quantitative synthesis. METHODS: The prespecified search logic for records published between 1 January 2010 and 28 February 2026 was completed on 23 July 2026 across PubMed/MEDLINE, ClinicalTrials.gov, Embase via Ovid, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials via Ovid. Phase II/III randomized trials were separated from early-phase biomarker trials, registry records, conference reports, press releases, and post-cut-off updates. Risk of bias was assessed with cochrane risk-of-bias 2 tools. "Protocol registration: www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero identifier is CRD420261333324." RESULTS: Four phase II trials contributed quantitative efficacy data (n CONCLUSION: Randomized evidence does not currently support disease modification by immune-based or inflammation-targeted therapy in PD. This translational paradox reflects incomplete central engagement due to risk or engagement without clinical benefit.

papers.title: Correlation between serum uric acid, homocysteine and cystatin C levels and Parkinson's disease.
papers.journal: Malawi medical journal : the journal of Medical Association of Malawi
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder associated with metabolic abnormalities. Serum biomarkers such as uric acid (UA), homocysteine (Hcy), and cystatin C (Cys-C) may be involved in its pathogenesis and progression. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the associations between serum UA, Hcy, and Cys-C levels and disease duration, severity, and cognitive function in patients with PD. METHODS: From January 2023 to December 2024, sixty patients diagnosed with PD and sixty age- and sex-matched healthy controls were enrolled. PD patients were further stratified by disease duration (<5 years vs. ≥5 years), Hoehn and Yahr (H&Y) stage (mild vs. moderate-to-severe), and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score (normal cognition vs. cognitive impairment). Serum levels of UA, Hcy, and Cys-C were compared among groups, and Pearson correlation analysis was performed to examine their relationships with disease duration, H&Y stage, and MoCA score. RESULTS: Compared with healthy controls, PD patients exhibited significantly higher serum Hcy and Cys-C levels and lower UA levels (all P<0.01). Patients with longer disease duration, higher H&Y stage, or cognitive impairment showed elevated Hcy and Cys-C levels and reduced UA levels (P<0.01 for all comparisons). Pearson correlation analysis revealed that UA was negatively correlated with disease duration (r = -0.757, P<0.001), H&Y stage (r = -0.869, P<0.001), and MoCA score (r = -0.606, P<0.001), while Hcy and Cys-C were positively correlated with these indicators (all P<0.01). CONCLUSION: Elevated serum Hcy and Cys-C and reduced UA levels are closely associated with PD progression and cognitive decline. These biomarkers may serve as valuable indicators for monitoring disease severity and guiding clinical management.

papers.title: Q-DOAS: A Proximity Quenching Assay for Real-Time Detection of Early Protein Aggregation Events.
papers.journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
papers.abstract: Protein aggregation is central to numerous neurodegenerative diseases. The paucity of facile assays to measure aggregation and detect amyloid seeds hinders therapeutics development and clinical assessments. The standard ThT assay reports on amyloid formation but is blind to early oligomers and is prone to interference. We describe Q-DOAS, a simple and reproducible assay that quantifies aggregation in real time via proximity-quenching of a site-specifically conjugated dye (BODIPY-TMR). Using mutant Huntingtin-exon 1 (mHTT-Ex1) and α-Synuclein A53T, we show Q-DOAS detects pre-amyloid oligomers, yielding quantitative kinetic data compatible with mechanistic analysis. We further demonstrate its utility to dissect mutational effects, screen for protein and small-molecule aggregation inhibitors, and quantify amyloid seeding activity in cellular and mouse models of Huntington's disease and in cerebrospinal fluid from Parkinson's disease patients without amplification. Q-DOAS provides a sensitive, robust, and scalable tool for studying the earliest events in amyloid pathologies and for advancing therapeutic development.

papers.title: Beyond the brain: curcumin as a multi-target neuropharmacological modulator of the gut-brain axis in major depressive disorder and Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Curcumin, the principal polyphenol of Curcuma longa, has been proposed as a multi-target neuropharmacological agent for neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders. We propose that major depressive disorder (MDD) and Parkinson's disease (PD) share a convergent gut-brain axis dysfunction, and that curcumin can serve as a pharmacological probe to test whether this convergent pathway is causally relevant. This narrative review evaluates that hypothesis. We conducted a structured literature search across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and CNKI using predefined search terms. This is a narrative review with a structured search strategy rather than a systematic review; no formal risk-of-bias assessment or meta-analysis was performed. From 2256 identified records, 112 primary studies were selected for synthesis after dual screening and consensus resolution. Findings should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than as a quantitative synthesis. We propose a differential metabolite-sensitivity threshold model as a testable hypothesis: shared dysbiosis-related metabolic and inflammatory disturbances may affect serotonergic function earlier than dopaminergic function because depressed mood manifests at modest neurotransmitter deficits, whereas nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons possess substantial compensatory reserve. Preclinical studies indicate that curcumin exerts prebiotic-like effects, promotes short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria, suppresses NF-κB-dependent neuroinflammation, restores BDNF signaling, inhibits α-synuclein aggregation, and improves depressive- and PD-like behaviors. These actions map onto convergent gut-brain pathways involving short-chain fatty acid deficiency, tryptophan-kynurenine imbalance, monoaminergic precursor depletion, and neuroinflammation. This model generates four testable predictions: (P1: functional dysbiosis convergence; P2: temporal precedence of depressed mood; P3: curcumin's multi-node modu

papers.title: GLP-1 receptor agonists as potential disease-modifying agents in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease: mechanisms, clinical trial evidence, and the neuroprotection horizon.
papers.abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), originally developed as antidiabetic agents, have emerged as candidate disease-modifying therapies for Parkinson's disease (PD) and Alzheimer's disease (AD), reflecting the widespread expression of GLP-1 receptors across neurons, glia, and the cerebral vasculature. This narrative review synthesizes mechanistic, clinical trial, and biomarker evidence for GLP-1 RAs in PD and AD, based on a literature search of PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science, with ClinicalTrials.gov searched separately for trial protocols and results, through May 2026. Preclinical data implicate GLP-1 receptor agonism in anti-neuroinflammatory signaling, mitochondrial preservation, autophagy and proteostasis enhancement, anti-apoptotic effects, synaptic plasticity, cerebrovascular protection, and glymphatic clearance. Clinical evidence in PD is mixed and agent- and formulation-dependent: the phase II Exenatide-PD trial reported a motor benefit that persisted after washout (∼3.5-point between-group difference in MDS-UPDRS Part III), and the phase II LIXIPARK trial (lixisenatide) reported a significant 3.08-point between-group difference (95% CI 0.86-5.30; p

papers.title: Diagnostic accuracy of Neuromelanin-sensitive MRI for Parkinson Disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Objective: The diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD) remains challenging due to clinical overlap with other parkinsonian syndromes and the absence of widely available imaging biomarkers. Neuromelanin-sensitive MRI (NM-MRI) enables in vivo visualization of neuromelanin in the substantia nigra (SN) and locus coeruleus (LC), where signal loss reflects dopaminergic neurodegeneration in the SN and noradrenergic neurodegeneration in the LC. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of NM-MRI in differentiating PD from healthy controls. MATERIALS AND METHODS: PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to February 2025. Studies evaluating the diagnostic accuracy of NM-MRI in PD versus healthy controls were included. Two independent reviewers extracted data and assessed methodological quality using QUADAS-2. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were estimated using a random-effects bivariate model, with construction of a summary receiver operating characteristic (SROC) curve. Subgroup analyses were performed by anatomical region (SN, LC) and imaging parameter (volume, area, signal intensity, contrast ratio, subjective assessment), along with meta-regression and Deeks' funnel plot for publication bias. This review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251088071). RESULTS: Twenty-eight studies comprising 2,268 participants were included. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were 88.0 % (95 % CI, 85.3-90.2 %) and 84.4 % (95 % CI, 80.6-87.5 %), respectively, with an area under the SROC curve of 0.901 and low heterogeneity (I2 CONCLUSION: NM-MRI demonstrates high diagnostic accuracy for differentiating PD from healthy controls, with volumetric analysis of the substantia nigra offering a robust and reproducible imaging biomarker. papers.title: The Testing of a Developed Voice Recognition System for the Clinical Diagnosis of Individuals With Parkinson's Disease.
papers.journal: Journal of voice : official journal of the Voice Foundation
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is frequently accompanied by speech and voice impairments, particularly dysarthria and dysphonia, which may emerge before motor symptoms become clinically apparent through conventional diagnostic criteria. This study tested a newly developed voice-recognition system designed to support the clinical diagnosis of PD through objective acoustic analysis. A total of 190 individuals with idiopathic PD (89 female, 101 male), diagnosed according to the UK Parkinson's Disease Society Brain Bank criteria, and 190 age- and sex-comparable healthy controls (114 female, 76 male), all native Turkish speakers, were recruited at Gülhane Training and Research Hospital. Voice recordings-sustained vowel phonation, a standardized reading passage, and spontaneous speech-were obtained under controlled acoustic conditions and analyzed in MATLAB, yielding 26 acoustic parameters, including fundamental frequency, jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio, formant frequencies, vowel space area, cepstral peak prominence, and mel-frequency cepstral coefficients. Between-group differences and correlations with Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS) scores were examined, and three machine-learning classifiers-k-NN, support vector machines, and multilayer perceptron-were trained using leave-one-out cross-validation. Participants with PD (mean age 64.5 ± 7.5 years; Hoehn & Yahr 2.45 ± 0.34; UPDRS 41.8 ± 6.2) differed significantly from healthy controls (mean age 61.2 ± 7.1 years) across multiple acoustic parameters, several of which correlated with UPDRS scores. The k-NN classifier achieved the best performance, distinguishing individuals with PD from controls with 97% accuracy (AUC = 0.957; F1 = 0.951). papers.title: Microbial metabolites as modulators of gut-brain communication in neurodegeneration: from intestinal sensing to disease initiation and progression.
papers.abstract: How heterogeneous gut metabolite alterations relate to Parkinson's disease (PD) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains unresolved. We propose a framework in which intestinal sensing of indole derivatives, short-chain fatty acids and bile acids links microbial function to barrier regulation and gut-brain communication. Integration denotes tissue-level convergence of aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR), pregnane X receptor (PXR) and metabolite-responsive G-protein-coupled receptor responses across epithelial and neighbouring immune cells, rather than an established same-cell receptor complex. Tryptophan metabolism provides an analytical focus connecting microbial indole production with host kynurenine and serotonin pathways; metabolite concentrations alone do not establish pathway flux or receptor activity. We hypothesise that suppressed indole-associated epithelial signalling, barrier hyperpermeability and peripheral immune activation could form a shared gut-derived vulnerability state in subsets of PD and AD. Its co-occurrence and temporal relationship to CNS pathology have not been prospectively demonstrated. Neural, immune and vascular processes may overlap in both diseases, with genotype and cellular context modifying relative susceptibility rather than determining exclusive pathways. Human observational findings are distinguished from experimental mechanisms and proposed interactions. Receptor-directed treatments and metabolite-based biomarkers remain candidates requiring mechanism-specific, safety and clinical validation. Whether a gut-derived intervention window exists, is reversible, or favours earlier treatment requires longitudinal and controlled studies. The framework accommodates bidirectional communication and CNS-intrinsic disease, and generates separate tests of composite gut phenotyping and genotype-metabolite interactions.

papers.title: Intrastriatal injection of amplified Lewy body dementia (LBD) fibrils in mice results in accumulation of fibrils with LBD structure and neurodegeneration.
papers.journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
papers.abstract: The defining neuropathologic feature of Lewy body dementia (LBD) and Parkinson's disease (PD) is alpha-synuclein (Asyn) fibril accumulation in Lewy bodies (LBs) and Lewy neurites (LNs). Recently, we developed a method to amplify Asyn fibrils derived from human post-mortem LBD brain tissue and determined that the structure of amplified Asyn fibrils is highly similar to the structure of fibrils directly isolated from LBD brain tissue. We examined whether injection of these fibrils into humanized Asyn mice recapitulates pathologic Asyn fibril accumulation with human LBD Asyn fibril structure. We utilized mice containing a null allele in the mouse Snca gene and a human SNCA transgene. Intrastriatal injection of amplified Asyn fibrils derived from 3 different LBD autopsy cases resulted in cytoplasmic and neuritic phospho-Asyn accumulation in the striatum, cortex, and amygdala bilaterally at 3mpi. Fibril injections produced a reduction in the number of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, with LB-like inclusions in surviving neurons, and produced impaired sensorimotor function as measured on the accelerating rotarod test. Fibril accumulation increased 3.6-fold between 1 and 3 months post-injection (mpi) and was relatively stable between 3 and 5 mpi. We amplified fibrils from mouse brain tissue 5 mpi and collected single-particle cryo-EM data. High resolution 3D structural information could not be obtained because of the lack of helical twist, but comparison of the cryo-EM 2D class averages with those derived from amplified fibrils prepared from human LBD tissue revealed multiple matching classes, indicating that the Lewy fold is maintained in the fibrils that accumulate in mouse brain tissue. Our findings demonstrate an approach to model the accumulation of Asyn fibrils with LBD structure in mice, providing a platform for investigating disease mechanisms, imaging biomarkers, and therapeutics targeting Asyn in PD/LBD.

papers.title: Examining the Relationship Between Regional Vulnerability and Psychotic-Like Experiences in Adolescents: The Potential Mediating Role of Cognition.
papers.journal: Biological psychiatry. Cognitive neuroscience and neuroimaging
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Psychotic-like experiences (PLEs) are subclinical hallucinations or unusual thought content that, when distressing or persistent, signal heightened risk for psychosis spectrum disorders and cognitive impairments. METHODS: We used data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study (N = ∼11,800) to examine if structural brain deviations toward neuropsychiatric disorders, quantified using disorder-specific Regional Vulnerability Indices (RVIs), were associated with distressing PLEs at age 13-14, and whether cognition mediated these relationships. Cortical and subcortical RVIs were calculated for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, metabolic disorder, and 22q11.2 deletion syndrome. RESULTS: Linear mixed-effects models revealed that higher cortical RVIs for schizophrenia, Alzheimer's disease, bipolar disorder, metabolic disorder, and Parkinson's disease-and all subcortical RVIs-were significantly associated with greater distressing PLE severity. Both cortical and subcortical RVIs were negatively associated with fluid and crystallized cognition, with subcortical RVIs showing the largest effects. Mediation analyses indicated that crystallized cognition, and to a lesser extent fluid cognition, mediated many RVI-distressing PLE relationships. DISCUSSION: These findings suggest that neuroanatomical differences confer risk for psychotic-like experiences partly through their impact on cognitive development. The results highlight RVIs as sensitive markers of distributed brain vulnerability in youth and suggest that cognitive function, particularly crystallized ability, is a potential pathway linking brain structural alterations to emerging psychotic symptoms.

papers.title: Aborted sudden cardiac death in children and adolescents-from acute management to diagnosis.
papers.abstract: Aborted sudden cardiac death (SCD) in children and adolescents is terrifying for patients and families. Inherited arrhythmia syndromes, cardiomyopathies, and coronary anomalies are the most common associations. This review provides a comprehensive framework for diagnostic evaluation in survivors of resuscitated sudden cardiac arrest. After hemodynamic stabilization and neuroprotection, evaluation often requires data retrieval, structured cardiac phenotyping, and obtaining samples to assess for molecular, metabolic or toxicology analysis. A tiered approach is essential. A surface electrocardiogram (ECG) and echocardiography remain first line investigations. Primary electrical diseases may be evident on a standard and modified ECG, including Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome, conduction abnormalities, myocardial ischemia, and some cardiac channelopathies. Early echocardiography assesses structural heart disease, cardiomyopathies and myocarditis. Special attention should be paid to anomalous origin of the coronary arteries and recent work has emphasized the importance of mitral annular disjunction. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, exercise stress testing, and drug provocation testing can be useful supplements to reveal concealed substrates. Genetic testing is vital for precision medicine and cascade family screening, often requiring a multidisciplinary team to assess variants of uncertain significance (VUS) and complex genomic findings. Ultimately, the critical step is genotype-phenotype correlation, where the team determines whether the genetic and clinical data reinforce one another to provide a diagnosis, refine treatment, and prevent future tragedies within affected families.

papers.title: Safety-First, Severity-Adapted Enhanced Recovery After Surgery for Patients with Neurodegenerative Disorders: A Narrative Review and Proposed Framework.
papers.abstract: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) pathways have been shown to improve perioperative outcomes in broad surgical populations. However, their safety, feasibility, and optimal adaptation remain uncertain in patients with neurodegenerative disorders (NDDs), particularly those with dementia and Parkinson's disease. These patients often present with cognitive impairment and disability, which pose major perioperative care challenges. Our narrative review elucidates the pathophysiological traits, perioperative risks, and medication-related complications of patients with NDDs. We determine potential risks related to standard ERAS components, outline important drug-drug interactions between frequently prescribed NDD medications and anesthetic agents. We also offer useful suggestions for preoperative evaluation, intraoperative management, postoperative recovery, and post-discharge rehabilitation. We then present a three‑tier severity‑adapted ERAS framework, in which patients are stratified into mild, moderate, or severe groups based on the Hoehn and Yahr staging scale for Parkinson's disease and the Clinical Dementia Rating for dementia. This framework provides recommendations for the retention, modification, or restriction of ERAS components. We postulate that in this vulnerable population, the stratified decision-making pathways may help preserve the benefits of enhanced recovery while reducing avoidable iatrogenic harm and improving clinical feasibility. This, however, represents a conceptual framework requiring prospective validation.

papers.title: How to determine the suitability of Parkinson's disease patients for device-aided therapies: a practical approach.
papers.abstract: Device‑aided therapies (DATs) are important treatment options for people with Parkinson's disease whose symptoms can no longer be adequately controlled with oral or transdermal medication. They offer the potential to maintain or restore quality of life when conventional approaches are insufficient. Identifying which individuals with PD should be referred for DAT assessment, and then selecting the most appropriate therapy for each individual, requires careful evaluation of multiple factors. These extend beyond efficacy and tolerability to include practical, real‑world considerations shaped by a person's personal circumstances, preferences, and care systems. To support clinicians in the initial step of recognizing when a person may be ready to transition to a DAT, several screening tools have been developed. Among these, D‑DATS is a practical, precise, and easy‑to‑use three‑factor tool designed for routine clinical practice. Validation studies indicate that D‑DATS outperforms commonly used criteria such as the '5‑2‑1' rule and MANAGE‑PD, with respect to its specificity, reducing unnecessary or premature referrals. This article reviews the importance of accurate selection of suitable people with PD using a precise tool such as D‑DATS, and explores the real‑world considerations that can help guide the choice between DAT options. As motor efficacy, expressed as the reduction in the number of daily OFF-time hours, is broadly comparable across all DATs, the final decision often hinges on additional factors, like safety, long-term maintenance, and practical and patient‑centered factors. To support this process, we propose a decision‑tree flow chart to help clinicians navigate therapy selection in partnership with their patients. papers.title: Stage-Specific Health Status in Multiple System Atrophy: EQ-5D Findings from a European Cohort.
papers.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Multiple system atrophy (MSA) is a rare neurodegenerative disorder that severely impairs health-related quality of life (HRQoL). Disease progression is assessed using the Unified Multiple System Atrophy Rating Scale Part IV (UMSARS IV), which defines five stages. However, stage-specific HRQoL estimates, particularly health-utility values, are unavailable. These estimates are essential for health-economic evaluation of treatments and for supporting HRQoL as a clinical trial endpoint. Bayesian methods offer a practical approach for analyzing HRQoL in rare diseases. OBJECTIVE: To estimate EQ-5D-based health-utility values across UMSARS IV stages in MSA. METHODS: EQ-5D data from the European MSA Study Group cohort were analyzed. EQ-5D-3L responses were mapped to EQ-5D-5L health-utility values using the German value set, where a value of 1 represents perfect health and lower or negative values indicate worse health. Bayesian modeling estimated stage-specific health-utility values, reporting posterior means and 95% credible intervals (CrI). Sensitivity analyses included alternative model specifications and imputations of missing UMSARS IV stages. RESULTS: Stage-specific EQ-5D-5L health-utility values were 0.672 (95% CrI 0.628-0.719) for UMSARS IV Stage 1, 0.606 (95% CrI 0.523-0.679) for Stage 2, 0.517 (95% CrI 0.416-0.615) for Stage 3, 0.262 (95% CrI 0.158-0.364) for Stage 4, and 0.084 (95% CrI -0.045 to 0.217) for Stage 5. Bayesian models demonstrated good fit, capturing variability within stages and across countries. Sensitivity analyses confirmed robustness, with health-utility values reflecting expected MSA progression. CONCLUSIONS: This study is the first to provide stage-specific health-utility values across all UMSARS IV stages, enabling health-economic evaluations of emerging interventions and supporting HRQoL as a clinical trial endpoint. © 2026 The Author(s). papers.abstract: Genome-wide association studies of Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies largely rely on clinical diagnoses, which can misclassify cases and cannot characterise the anatomical distribution of Lewy pathology. Autopsy cohorts allow identification of variants associated both with developing Lewy body disease and with the neocortical extent of its pathology. We meta-analysed genome-wide data from 2,661 individuals of European ancestry with autopsy-confirmed Lewy body disease and 12,068 controls (2,124 autopsy-confirmed) from the Global Parkinson's Genetics Program (GP2) and the National Institutes of Health NeuroBioBank, and estimated genetic correlation with clinically diagnosed Alzheimer's disease. In 2,309 cases from the GP2 and the Mayo Clinic Jacksonville Brain Bank, we compared neocortical (n = 1,362) with brainstem or limbic (n = 947) Lewy pathology, adjusting for Alzheimer's disease co-pathology, age at death and sex.
